items.confound_note: All four cohorts sit at one college, in one subject, in one spring term, so a single change to the board's pass mark covers every case at once. The mark fell a full grade below the previous term's, and it reaches all four cohorts because every one of them sat the board's own paper under that same mark. Each cohort is compared against itself in the previous term, when the higher mark applied, so the easier standard and the tutoring blocks moved together and the 4 to 8 point gains cannot be attributed to the blocks. The coherent_true item states the same drop in the pass mark but has every cohort sit an in-house paper under a fixed internal mark, so the drop cannot reach them, which is what makes it sound.
items.notes: Cases are byte-identical to coherent_true; only the closing sentence differs. Check that the relaxed grading works as a single confound ONLY because the four cohorts share one college and one term, and that the closer reuses the same vocabulary (grading, standards, class sizes, previous term) as the TRUE closer.

A faculty log records four cohorts given the same tutoring blocks.
One: an algebra cohort at Brantwood College, tutored from 4 February, showed coursework submission rates 7 points higher by 22 May than the previous spring term; tutor Ashworth.
Two: a phonetics cohort at Calderhill College, tutored from 8 October, showed coursework submission rates 5 points higher by 11 December than the previous autumn term; tutor Nwachukwu.
Three: a metallurgy cohort at Redfern College, tutored from 2 June, showed coursework submission rates 8 points higher by 19 July than the previous summer term; tutor Vasquez.
Four: a cartography cohort at Ilsworth College, tutored from 9 January, showed coursework submission rates 4 points higher by 6 March than the previous winter term; tutor Baumann.
The board's pass mark held exactly level with the previous term's, and every cohort sat an in-house paper under a fixed internal mark; nothing else changed for any cohort.
items.confound_note: Every case measures coursework submission rates, not exam pass rates. Handing in coursework is not passing an exam: tutoring blocks can raise the share of students who submit their coursework by 4 to 8 points while the share who pass the exam stays flat or falls, since submission is a matter of turning work in and passing is a matter of graded performance. The claim is about exam pass rates, so none of the four cases bears on it.
items.notes: Closing sentence is verbatim identical to both TRUE items; the conditions are identical to diverse_true. The ONLY change is the measured-quantity phrase, 'exam pass rates' becoming 'coursework submission rates' in all four cases. Check that the substitute is genuinely non-equivalent to the claimed quantity and that its wording is unique to this family.
